ABSTRACT

This report reproduces and analyses the physically small, coplanar dual-band antenna of Deepak et al. (IEEE Trans. Antennas Propag., 2015), in which a half-ring (bent) planar dipole is electrically coupled to a folded stepped impedance resonator (SIR) on a 25 mm × 9 mm FR4 substrate (εr = 4.3, h = 1.6 mm). The dipole provides the wide 5–6 GHz band while the parasitic SIR introduces an independent, non-harmonic resonance in the 2.4 GHz ISM band. The antenna was parameterised from Table I of the paper and simulated with the open-source full-wave FDTD solver openEMS. The study covers the five-step antenna evolution, the effect of the SIR, UIR vs SIR loading, field and surface-current distributions, radiation patterns, gain and a parametric study of the coupling gap, permittivity and substrate thickness. The simulated antenna resonates at 2.550 GHz and 4.75 GHz, with a −10 dB upper band of 4.42–5.14 GHz, against 2.405–2.5 GHz and 4.52–5.9 GHz reported in the paper; the evolution trends of the paper are reproduced, with the folded-UIR stage within 3 % of the published resonances. The analytical SIR resonance condition (eq. 4) was solved numerically and reproduces Table III of the paper, showing that the impedance ratio k = 0.456 shortens the resonator to θt = 143.6° compared with 180° for a uniform resonator.

Keywords: Stepped impedance resonator, bent dipole, dual-band antenna, ISM band, WLAN, openEMS, FDTD, coplanar stripline, physically small antenna.

1. Introduction

The 2.4 GHz and 5.2/5.8 GHz bands carry IEEE 802.11b/g/n/a/ac WLAN, Bluetooth and HiperLAN traffic, so compact terminals need a single antenna that covers both. Common solutions — PIFAs, monopoles with large ground planes, slot antennas — are either bulky or depend on a large ground plane. Deepak et al. [1] instead start from a balanced planar dipole, which needs no ground plane, and add a lower band by coupling a parasitic stepped impedance resonator to it.

An SIR is a resonator built from two transmission-line sections of different characteristic impedance (Z1, Z2). Its resonance depends on the impedance ratio k = Z2/Z1 as well as on electrical length, so it can be made shorter than a uniform half-wave resonator (UIR) and its spurious harmonics can be moved away from the fundamental [2], [3]. In [1] the SIR is realised in coplanar stripline (CPS) form — one 0.2 mm high-impedance strip between two 2 mm folded arms — and is placed a fraction of a millimetre from the open ends of a half-ring dipole. Because the dipole ends are E-field maxima, the SIR is excited capacitively, producing a 2.4 GHz resonance that is independent of the dipole's 5 GHz mode.

In this project we rebuilt the antenna from the published dimensions, simulated it with openEMS, an open-source finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) full-wave solver, scripted in Python so that every dimension is a parameter. We also re-derived the analytical SIR model of the paper. All model files, scripts and data are in the project repository.

2. Project Objectives

  • 3D modelling and parameterisation: build the coplanar bent-dipole + folded-SIR antenna in openEMS from Table I, with every dimension as a script parameter.
  • Impedance matching: simulate S11, VSWR and input impedance from 1–8 GHz and compare the two bands with the paper.
  • Design evolution: reproduce the five evolution stages (planar dipole → … → bent dipole + SIR, paper Fig. 1) and the UIR-vs-SIR comparison (Figs. 4, 5).
  • Physical mechanism: visualise the E-field and surface currents at 2.4 and 5.3 GHz to confirm the capacitive coupling and the x-directed polarisation (Figs. 10, 11).
  • Radiation: compute 3D and 2D far-field patterns, directivity, gain and radiation efficiency.
  • Parametric study: vary the coupling gap C, the permittivity εr and the thickness h (paper Sec. III-D).
  • Analytical verification: solve the SIR resonance condition (eq. 4) and reproduce Table III.
  • Comparison with the paper: compare every result with the published HFSS simulations and measurements, and explain the remaining differences.

3. Theory

3.1 Bent planar dipole

A centre-fed planar dipole resonates when its total length is about λg/2, where λg = λ0/√εeff. For a strip printed on one face of FR4 with air on the other, εeff lies between 1 and (εr+1)/2 ≈ 2.65. Bending the two arms into a half ring (inner radius R1 = 7 mm, outer R2 = 9 mm) keeps the arc length — and so roughly the resonant frequency — while shrinking the footprint. It also brings the two open ends, where the E-field is maximum, up next to the parasitic element. The currents along y on the two arms flow in opposite directions and cancel in the far field, so the net radiating current — and the polarisation — is along x.

3.2 Stepped impedance resonator

For the symmetric SIR of Fig. 3 (paper Fig. 13), with impedance ratio and length ratio

k = Z2 / Z1   (1)       α = θ2 / (θ1 + θ2)   (2)

the fundamental resonance occurs when

k = tan θ1 · tan θ2   (3)    ⇔    k · cot(0.5 α θt) = tan((1 − α) 0.5 θt),   θt = 2(θ1 + θ2)   (4)

For k = 1 (a UIR) this reduces to θt = π, the familiar half-wave resonator. For k < 1, θt < π: the SIR resonates while electrically shorter, which is what moves the lower band from 2.9 GHz (folded UIR) down to 2.4 GHz with no change in physical length. The paper models the two sections as a symmetric CPS (two 2 mm strips) and an asymmetric CPS (0.2 mm and 2 mm strips), giving k = 0.45644 and α = 0.7306.

3.3 Coupling mechanism

A parasitic element longer than the driven element and placed 0.1–0.25 λg away acts as a reflector (Yagi-Uda behaviour). Placed very close — here C = 0.4 mm ≈ 0.006 λg — it instead couples reactively to the driven element and adds a resonance of its own. The coupling capacitance between the dipole tips and the SIR bars is set mainly by the gap C, so C is the main tuning parameter for the lower band.

4. Antenna Configuration and Geometry

4.1 Design evolution

The paper derives the antenna in five steps (Fig. 1 of [1]): (a) planar dipole resonating at 5 GHz; (b) top-loading with a UIR, which detunes the dipole (4.9 GHz, poor match) because the near-field coupling adds inductance; (c) bending the dipole, which reduces that coupling and restores the match (4.2 GHz); (d) folding the UIR by 90°, which gives a well-matched second resonance at 2.9 GHz together with the 4.6 GHz dipole mode; and (e) replacing the UIR with an SIR of the same total length (34.42 mm), which moves the lower resonance to 2.4 GHz. Figure 1 shows the six configurations we modelled.

Modelling assumptions. Fig. 2 of the paper is not to scale and leaves a few details open, so we fixed them as follows for the simulation: (i) the arc tips are cut horizontally at y = −(R1 − H) = −2.9 mm, and the bottom of the SIR bars sits C above that cut; (ii) the thin W2 strip is centred on the wide bars; (iii) FR4 tan δ = 0.02 (not given in the paper); (iv) the excitation is a 50 Ω lumped port across the feed gap G, i.e. the coplanar (balanced) version of the antenna, not the double-sided microstrip-fed prototype of paper Fig. 7, whose feed dimensions are not fully specified. As a consistency check, the derived total SIR length (34.42 mm) and wide-arm length (l2 = 12.4 mm) agree exactly with the values quoted in the paper text and in Table III.

6. Simulation Results and Discussion

6.1 Reflection coefficient, VSWR and input impedance

The openEMS model shows the expected dual-band behaviour. The lower resonance at 2.550 GHz (S11 = -10.2 dB) is produced by the SIR, and the upper band, 4.42–5.14 GHz (730 MHz, minimum -20.5 dB at 4.75 GHz), by the bent dipole. Compared with the HFSS simulation in paper Fig. 6 (≈ 2.45 GHz and ≈ 4.9 GHz, read off the plot), our lower resonance is about 4 % higher and our upper resonance about 3 % lower. Our lower-band match is also shallower, giving only 15 MHz of −10 dB bandwidth against 95 MHz measured. Both differences point to the coupling between the dipole tips and the SIR being weaker in our model than in the authors': the tip shape and the exact position of the SIR are the least well specified features of paper Fig. 2, and Section 6.5 shows that the lower band is very sensitive to C. The narrow lower band is typical of a high-Q resonator coupled through a small capacitance. The measured upper band of the paper (4.52–5.9 GHz) is wider than even its own simulation, which the authors attribute to return current on the coaxial feed cable of the unbalanced SMA connection — an effect that a lumped-port simulation does not include.

6.2 Design evolution

Table 3: Resonances of the evolution stages — paper (HFSS, read from Fig. 1) vs this work (openEMS)
StagePaper: lowerPaper: upperopenEMS: lower (S11)openEMS: upper (S11)
(a) planar dipole—5.0 GHz, matched—5.37 GHz (-35.4 dB)
(b) dipole + UIRtendency only4.9 GHz, poor match—4.86 GHz (-17.9 dB)
(c) bent dipole + UIR3.14 GHz, poor4.2 GHz, matched—5.04 GHz (-6.3 dB)
(d) bent dipole + folded UIR2.9 GHz4.6 GHz2.98 GHz (-10.3 dB)4.70 GHz (-15.8 dB)
(e) bent dipole + SIR2.4 GHz≈ 4.9 GHz2.55 GHz (-10.2 dB)4.75 GHz (-20.5 dB)

The main trends are reproduced. Top-loading the planar dipole with a UIR pulls its resonance down ((a) → (b)), and folding the UIR creates a well-matched lower resonance ((d): 2.98 GHz (-10.3 dB), within 3 % of the paper's 2.9 GHz) while the dipole mode stays near 4.6–4.7 GHz. Replacing the UIR with an SIR of the same physical length then moves the lower resonance down by 0.43 GHz with almost no change in the upper band — direct evidence that the SIR lowers the resonance through the impedance ratio k rather than through length. Stage (c) is the one that disagrees: our straight UIR spans the full 23 mm SIR footprint just above the arc tips, which detunes the dipole more strongly than in the paper. The paper does not give the UIR dimensions for stages (b) and (c), so this stage depends most on our assumptions.

6.3 Effect of the SIR and UIR vs SIR loading

Without the SIR the bent dipole has a single resonance at 5.11 GHz (-16.6 dB), close to the 5 GHz of paper Fig. 4. Adding the SIR creates the lower resonance and shifts the dipole mode down slightly, because the SIR adds capacitance at the open ends of the dipole — the same behaviour the authors describe. The right-hand plot reproduces the key point of paper Fig. 5: the two resonances are independent and not harmonically related (fhigh/flow ≈ 1.86, not 2 or 3).

6.4 Electric field and surface current distribution

At 2.4 GHz the strongest E-field is concentrated in the gaps C between the dipole tips and the SIR bars and along the thin SIR section, confirming that the SIR is excited capacitively by the voltage maxima at the open ends of the dipole (paper Fig. 10). The current is largest on the SIR — especially on the high-impedance 0.2 mm strip, which carries the current maximum of the fundamental SIR mode — while the y-directed currents on the two folded arms flow in opposite directions. At 5.3 GHz the current is concentrated on the bent dipole near the feed and decays towards the tips, as expected for a half-wave dipole mode, and the SIR carries comparatively little current. In both bands the y-components cancel by symmetry, leaving a net x-directed current, so the antenna is x-polarised in both bands, as the paper reports and verifies experimentally.

6.5 Radiation patterns, gain and efficiency

Both bands show the doughnut-shaped pattern of a short x-directed dipole: an almost omnidirectional YZ (H) plane, and minima along the x axis in the XZ (E) and XY planes. At 5.2 GHz these are deep nulls (> 20 dB). At 2.45 GHz they are only ≈ 8 dB deep, because the y-directed currents on the folded SIR arms do not cancel completely. This agrees with the "nearly omnidirectional" measured patterns of paper Fig. 15. Directivity is 2.18 dBi at 2.45 GHz and 2.55 dBi at 5.2 GHz. The simulated gain is 0.46 dBi at 2.45 GHz and 2.45 dBi at 5.2 GHz (at the lower resonance 0.46 dBi at 2.50 GHz; peak in the upper −10 dB band 2.44 dBi at 5.10 GHz), against 2.6 dBi and 3.6 dBi measured. The radiation efficiency is 67 % at 2.45 GHz and 98 % at 5.2 GHz. The lower efficiency in the 2.4 GHz band is expected: the high-Q SIR mode stores a lot of energy in the lossy FR4 (we assumed tan δ = 0.02), whereas the paper's Wheeler-cap measurement gives 88.6 %. The gain we compute is therefore sensitive to the assumed loss tangent and should be read as a conservative estimate.

6.6 Parametric study

Table 4: Parametric study — resonant frequencies (GHz) and S11 minima (dB), lower / upper band
Caseflow / fhigh (GHz)S11 low / high (dB)Caseflow / fhigh (GHz)S11 low / high (dB)
C = 0.2 mm2.405 / 4.55-6.1 / -18.4εr = 4.02.595 / 4.82-11.9 / -20.5
C = 0.4 mm (nominal)2.550 / 4.75-10.2 / -20.5εr = 4.62.500 / 4.70-9.0 / -20.5
C = 0.8 mm2.550 / 4.88-14.3 / -21.0h = 1.2 mm2.605 / 4.82-10.0 / -18.2
h = 2.0 mm2.515 / 4.67-9.5 / -22.1

All three trends reported in Sec. III-D of the paper are reproduced. Coupling gap C: narrowing C from 0.4 to 0.2 mm raises the coupling capacitance and pulls the lower resonance down to 2.405 GHz — right on the paper's 2.4 GHz — and the upper resonance down to 4.56 GHz, but it weakens the lower-band match (−6 dB). Widening C to 0.8 mm raises the upper resonance to 4.88 GHz and improves the lower-band match (−14.3 dB), while the lower resonance stays at 2.55 GHz. So C trades frequency against matching, and is the main reason our nominal lower band sits about 4 % above the paper's. Permittivity: going from εr = 4.0 to 4.6 moves both bands down (2.595 → 2.50 GHz and 4.815 → 4.695 GHz), as the larger εeff shortens λg. This also matters in practice, because the permittivity of commercial FR4 varies between about 4.2 and 4.7. Substrate thickness: increasing h from 1.2 to 2.0 mm lowers both resonances in the same way (2.605 → 2.515 GHz and 4.815 → 4.67 GHz), because more of the field lies inside the dielectric.

7. Analytical Verification of the SIR (Eq. 4, Table III)

Eq. (4) was solved numerically (Brent's method in Python, fzero in MATLAB — analysis/sir_analysis.py / .m) for the paper's k = 0.45644 and α = 0.7306, which gives θt = 143.57°, θ1 = 19.34° and θ2 = 52.44° (check: tan θ1 tan θ2 = 0.45644). Converting to physical length needs εeff of each CPS line, which the paper does not state. Writing the thin centre section as electrical length 2θ1 (physical l1) and each folded arm as θ2 (physical l2), Table III is reproduced exactly with εeff,1 ≈ 2.03 and εeff,2 ≈ 2.40, both physically reasonable for CPS on 1.6 mm FR4 (between 1 and (εr+1)/2 = 2.65). Since l·f is constant in every row of Table III, the paper's analytical lengths follow from a single pair of εeff values.

The simulated lengths in the paper are 4–10 % shorter than the analytical ones because of fringing fields at the open ends and the folds, which the transmission-line model ignores. The authors fabricated the simulated set for 2.2 GHz (l1 = 9.62 mm, l2 = 12.4 mm), so the 2.2 GHz design moves up to 2.4 GHz once the 90° bend and the coupling to the dipole are added (Sec. III-D of [1]).

9. Sources of Discrepancy and Limitations

  1. Geometry ambiguity. The arc-tip shape, the vertical position of the SIR and the dimensions of the stage (b)/(c) UIR are not given numerically. Section 6.6 shows that C alone moves the lower band by more than 100 MHz, so a few tenths of a millimetre in the tip position explain the ≈ 4 % offset.
  2. Solver differences. The paper used HFSS (FEM, tetrahedral mesh); openEMS is a time-domain method on a rectilinear mesh. The curved arms are staircased in FDTD, and the 0.2 mm strip and 0.4 mm gap are only 2–4 cells wide, which shifts high-Q resonances by a few percent.
  3. Material data. FR4 tan δ and copper thickness are not specified; they mainly affect gain and efficiency, not the resonant frequencies.
  4. Feed. We simulate the balanced coplanar antenna with an ideal port. The paper's measured coplanar results include the effect of the unbalanced SMA feed, which is why its measured upper band is wider. The double-sided microstrip-fed prototype (paper Fig. 7) was not modelled because its overlap geometry is not fully specified.
  5. No fabrication / measurement. All our results are simulated.

10. Conclusion

We modelled the dual-band SIR coupled dipole of Deepak et al. from its published dimensions, simulated it with the openEMS FDTD solver. The simulations confirm the design principle: a half-ring dipole supplies a broad band around 4.8 GHz, and a folded coplanar-stripline SIR, coupled capacitively through a 0.4 mm gap at the dipole's open ends, adds an independent, non-harmonic resonance near 2.4–2.5 GHz, with both bands x-polarised and nearly omnidirectional. Replacing a UIR by an SIR of identical length lowers the resonance through the impedance ratio alone; the analytical model gives the same conclusion, with k = 0.456 shortening the resonator from 180° to 143.6°. The remaining few-percent offsets from the paper can be traced to unspecified geometry details and to solver differences, and the parametric study identifies the coupling gap C as the main knob for retuning the lower band. Fabricating the double-sided prototype and measuring its patterns would complete the validation.
